catalog_quote: (a) a estrutura de uma palavra lexical simples é: / # (CV) ˈCVC # / por exemplo: / ˈkɔm / → [ ˈkˣɔm̚] água; / kiˈnam / → [ cçiˈnam̚] jaguar; ou / # (CV) ˈCVː # / por exemplo: / ˈkɔː / → [ ˈkˣɔ(ː)] puxar a corda do arco; / kuˈkiː / → [ kˣʊˈcçi(ː)] piranha. Em outros termos, a palavra lexical simples é sempre constituída de uma sílaba acentuada pesada (ou seja, tem uma rima bimoráica VC ou V:), eventualmente precedida de uma sílaba átona leve (ou seja, que tem uma rima monomoráica V). (b) estrutura de uma palavra gramatical simples: /# ˈCVC (–ʔçX) # / ... ou / # ˈCV: (–ʔçX) # / ... Em outros termos, a palavra gramatical simples superficial é sempre constituída de uma única sílaba acentuada pesada, que seja ela subjacente ou resultado da fusão de morfemas radical e afixal. [p.5] – seja de uma sequência de palavras simples, onde aquela que antecede a última palavra é acentuada e separada da última palavra por um limite interno "forte" ≠: / # (ω =) ˈω ≠ ω # / exemplos: /ˈsɛː≠ˈmɛː/ → [ ˈsɛː mɛ] jacaré [Angenot-de Lima & Angenot 2000: 157] Nas línguas Chapakura, a acentuação dos lexemas é dedutível do peso silábico - o único fator prosódico com papel fonológico nessa família lingüística. Portanto, o acento não é fonológico por ser previsível.

new_statements.translation: (a) the structure of a simple lexical word is /#(CV)ˈCVC#/, e.g. /ˈkɔm/ 'water', /kiˈnam/ 'jaguar'; or /#(CV)ˈCV:#/, e.g. /ˈkɔ:/ 'pull the bowstring', /kuˈki:/ 'piranha'. In other words, the simple lexical word always consists of a stressed heavy syllable (i.e. with a bimoraic rhyme VC or V:), optionally preceded by an unstressed light syllable (i.e. with a monomoraic rhyme V). [...] In other words, the surface simple grammatical word always consists of a single stressed heavy syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are maximally disyllabic (CV).CVC or (CV).CV; stress falls on the obligatory heavy (bimoraic) syllable, which is always word-final, so the light CV first syllable of a disyllable is unstressed. Stress is thus predictable from syllable weight (and equivalently word-final); Angenot-de Lima & Angenot 2000 state it is non-contrastive in all Chapakura languages and instrumentally confirm for Kuyubi that intensity prominence sits on the heavy final syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described for simple words. In compound lexical words with a 'strong' internal boundary (≠) the word preceding the last keeps its stress (/#(ω=)ˈω≠ω#/, e.g. [ˈsɛ: mɛ] 'jacaré'); no secondary-stress tier is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: Deaccentuation rules: a stressed syllable becomes unstressed before an affix boundary (A1.1, p.16), before a 'weak' internal boundary of a compound (A2.10a, p.20: only the last constituent keeps stress, e.g. [na ma ˈkxɔn] 'homem'), after a 'strong' compound boundary (A2.10b), and within utterances (B2a). Angenot-de Lima & Angenot 2000 p.156 note that in Kuyubi pitch (as opposed to intensity) prominence on the heavy syllable is of the 'frágil' (plateau-final) type except when the lexeme begins with a glottal stop.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the lexeme / phonological word (língua isolante; lexemes mono- or disyllabic); citation forms in hyperarticulated register. Compounds and utterance-level deaccentuation treated separately (pp.5, 16, 20, 29ff). The thesis frames Kaw Tayo as a dialect of Moré; Glottolog treats it as the separate language Kuyubi (kuyu1236).
new_statements.identity_note: Rodrigues Duran 2000 describes 'Kaw Tayo (Kujubi)', framed as the Brazilian dialect of Moré (Angenot-de Lima 2002 §2.3.4 likewise: 'dialecte moré-kaw tayo du Brésil'); Glottolog classifies this variety as the distinct language Kuyubi [kuyu1236] (sister of Moré/Itene iten1243 within Kujubim-More), and the etnolinguistica record and Birchall et al. 2016 ('Cojubim, also Kaw Tayo, Cautario, or Kuyubí') confirm the identity. Data from the last 2-3 elderly speakers (Suzana, Rosa, Francisca), recorded 1994-1999 in Guajará-Mirim/Sagarana. Note the same PDF was earlier saved under by the Itene search, flagged there as belonging to kuyu1236.

sources.note: Catalog kuyu1236: weight, rule 01, heavy VC/Vː + diphthong (already citing this paper p. 150). Paper confirms stress on the heavy lexeme-final syllable; intensity robustly on the heavy syllable, pitch prominence only 'frágil' (plateau-final, recovered by declination correction) except after a glottal onset. The catalog's Kuyubi means (11.8/21.1 dB, 42.5/43.8 ST, 126/205/322 ms, attributed to Duran 2000 p. 5) equal the glottal-onset row of table 1 here, not the general row.
